utterance: Set a timer for 20 minutes.
note: The spike's headline failure, re-expressed against the production schema. It answered duration_seconds: 20 for this utterance, which was a 60x error against the toy schema and is the CORRECT value here, because set_timer takes minutes. The failure does not transfer; the case is kept because it is the most common timer utterance there is.

utterance: Set a timer for two hours.
Set a timer for 90 seconds.
note: Downward conversion, and the hard direction: minutes is a number, not an integer, so 1.5 is representable and 1 or 2 is wrong. A model that only ever multiplies will fail this one.

utterance: Timer for half an hour.
Metti un timer di venti minuti.
Wake me at 7:30 tomorrow.
note: `date` is optional and is NOT expected here. "Tomorrow" is a relative day, and resolving it to a calendar date is the deterministic scheduling layer's job against the device clock — a model-produced date is refused by the grounding guard anyway.

utterance: wake me at seven thirty
note: Speech-to-text: no punctuation, no capitals, spelled-out numerals. Vesta's assist surface produces text like this routinely.

utterance: Set an alarm for 6am called gym.
Remind me to call the dentist at 3pm.
note: The schema's datetime format is ISO-8601, and the router is NOT expected to produce one: it has no date. It proposes the time the user said and the deterministic layer builds the absolute value. An ISO timestamp invented here would be a fabricated date wearing a format.

utterance: Ricordami di chiamare il dentista alle 15.
Put lunch with Sara on my calendar for Friday at noon.
note: Both required arguments present. `start` carries the user's own day and time tokens; turning "Friday at noon" into an ISO instant is the scheduling parser's job, and it already does it (lib/scheduling/parse.ts).

utterance: Navigate to Piazza Garibaldi.
What's Marco's number?
note: A read tool: it returns data a second generation answers from. Selecting it is not an irreversible action, which is why it is not tagged high-cost even though it names a person.

utterance: Call Marco.
Text Marco that I'm running late.
What's on my calendar?
note: The case that argues for an optional `date`. The utterance names no day, so the correct call carries NO date and Vesta resolves it to today at dispatch. A model that emits a date here has invented one, and the grounding guard refuses it — so an invented date turns a working request into a refusal.

utterance: What do I have on Thursday?
note: The pair to the case above: here the user DID name a day, so passing it is grounded and correct.

utterance: What does my insurance policy say about excess?
What time is it in Tokyo?
note: Vesta's deterministic world-time layer answers most of these before any model runs. The case is kept because the router must still be right about the ones that layer declines.

utterance: Set a timer for 30 seconds.
note: The sub-minute case. `minutes` is a number and 0.5 is representable; the dispatcher rounds minutes*60 to whole seconds, so 0.5 is exactly 30 seconds and 0 or 1 is a different timer. A model that only ever emits integers cannot pass this one.

utterance: Set a timer for 1 minute 30 seconds.
note: Two units in one duration, which is how people say a ninety-second timer out loud. The failure to watch for is concatenation rather than conversion — 130 instead of 1.5 — and the base model does exactly that.
